title: Four Black Tudor lives: Blanke, Francis, Diego and Fillis

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Four people, four very different journeys: a royal trumpeter, a salvage diver, a sailor who crossed the world with Drake, and a Moroccan woman who chose to be baptised in London. Their stories tell us a great deal about Tudor England.

blocks.p: John Blanke first appears in royal accounts in November 1507 as "John Blanke the blacke Trumpet", paid 8d a day, more than the standard 6d.
He may have arrived with Catherine of Aragon in 1501, but no record proves it. He played at Henry VII's funeral and Henry VIII's coronation in 1509.
He petitioned Henry VIII for a pay rise, asking for the post of a trumpeter who had died, Dominic Justinian. The king approved it.

He appears twice in the Westminster Tournament Roll of 1511, the only known portrait of a Black Tudor. In January 1512 Henry VIII gave him cloth for his wedding clothes, including violet cloth, a hat and a bonnet. After 1512 he disappears from the records.
Jacques Francis was born around 1527, probably on Arguin Island off Mauritania, West Africa, where diving skills were common.

He worked for Piero Paolo Corsi, a Venetian salvage contractor in Southampton, who called him his best diver. In 1546 Corsi's team was hired to recover guns from the wreck of the Mary Rose, which sank in 1545.

When Corsi was accused of stealing tin from another wreck, Francis gave evidence in the High Court of Admiralty on 8 February 1548, through an interpreter. He is the first known African to give evidence in an English court.
Opponents tried to dismiss him as a "slave" and an "infidel", but the court accepted his evidence. He called himself Corsi's "famulus", a servant, and evidence suggests he was paid.

sections.title: 3. Diego, circumnavigator

blocks.p: In 1572 Diego, who had escaped Spanish enslavement, ran through gunfire to reach Francis Drake's men at Nombre de Dios, Panama.
He helped the English ally with the Cimarrons, Africans who had escaped Spanish slavery, and together they captured a Spanish mule train carrying silver and gold.

He came to Plymouth with Drake and lived there for about four years. In November 1577 he sailed with Drake on the voyage around the world, serving as Drake's manservant and as an interpreter, since he spoke Spanish and English.

In November 1578 he was badly wounded by arrows on Mocha Island off Chile. He died of his wounds in 1579, near the Moluccas (Spice Islands). Evidence suggests he served under a contract, like other crew members.

evidence: Joined Drake 1572; sailed from Plymouth November 1577.

blocks.p: Mary Fillis was the daughter of Fillis of Morisco, a Moroccan basket weaver and shovel maker. She came to London around 1583, aged about six or seven.
She worked as a servant for John Barker, a merchant, and later for Millicent Porter, a seamstress in East Smithfield.

In 1597, around the age of 20, she asked to be baptised. The ceremony took place at St Botolph's, Aldgate. Choosing baptism suggests she wanted to belong to her community; it may also have helped her future.
She lived in London while Morocco and England were building an alliance against Spain. After Porter died in 1599, we do not know what happened to her.

misconceptions.wrong: John Blanke was a slave at court.
misconceptions.right: He was paid wages, petitioned for a pay rise and got it.

misconceptions.wrong: Africans could not give evidence in Tudor courts.
misconceptions.right: Jacques Francis gave evidence in 1548 and the court accepted it.
He had escaped slavery, and evidence suggests he served under a contract like other crew members.

misconceptions.wrong: Baptism meant someone was forced to convert.
misconceptions.right: Mary Fillis asked to be baptised.

sources.title: Westminster Tournament Roll
sources.origin: Made to record the tournament celebrating the birth of Henry VIII's son; held by the College of Arms.
sources.purpose: A celebration of royal display and the tournament.
sources.usefulness: Shows John Blanke twice, the only known image of a Black Tudor. It shows him in his role, not his thoughts.

sources.title: John Blanke's petition to Henry VIII
sources.origin: Royal records, held by The National Archives.
sources.purpose: To ask for higher wages and a dead trumpeter's post.
sources.usefulness: Rare evidence of a Black Tudor making a request in his own name. A clerk probably wrote it down for him.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that John Blanke was a valued, paid member of the royal court.
evidence.model: He was paid 8d a day from 1507, more than the standard 6d, won a pay rise after petitioning Henry VIII, and received a wedding gift of cloth in January 1512.

evidence.q: Explain what Jacques Francis's court case tells us about the status of Africans in Tudor England.
evidence.model: Opponents called him a slave and an infidel to discredit him, but the court accepted his evidence in 1548, which suggests Africans could be treated as free people with a voice in law.

I can describe the lives of Jacques Francis, Diego and Mary Fillis.

I can judge whose story is most significant for understanding Black Tudors.

questions.q: What does the life of John Blanke tell us about the position of Africans at the Tudor court?
questions.asks: Use precise evidence from Blanke's life to explain what it reveals, and its limits.
steps: Give evidence of wages and the petition.
Use the Tournament Roll and wedding gift.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 7 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

steps: Choose your strongest story and explain what it reveals.
Compare with at least one other story.

stretch.task: Which of the four do we come closest to hearing in their own words? What stops us hearing them more?
Map Jacques Francis's journey. What does it show about Tudor England's links to the wider world?
Drake is famous; Diego is not. Why might that be, and should it change?
Why might Mary Fillis have chosen baptism? Give two possible reasons and say which the evidence supports better.
